title: Which branches contain this fix?
summary: A security fix landed on main. Three release branches are live. Answer — without guessing — which of them already have it and which still need it.
mental_model: 'Does branch X have commit C?' is the reachability question, and `branch --contains` answers it exactly. 'Does X have an equivalent change?' is a different question, because cherry-picks and rebases change shas — that one needs `git cherry`.

commit.message: Fix timing attack in auth check

steps.title: Find the commit you care about
steps.why: Start from the fix itself. Every question below is phrased in terms of this sha, so capture it first — by message, not by scrolling.

steps.title: Ask which branches contain it
steps.why: `branch --contains <sha>` lists every branch from which that commit is reachable. This is the definitive answer, and it takes a second — far better than diffing files and guessing.
steps.expect: main contains it; both release branches do not.

verify.label: two release branches are missing the fix

steps.title: Backport it to one release
steps.why: `cherry-pick` copies the change onto another branch as a new commit with a different sha. The content is the same; the identity is not — which is what makes the next step interesting.

steps.title: Watch --contains give the wrong impression
steps.why: The cherry-picked commit has a different sha, so `--contains` still says release/1.1 does not contain the original. Reachability is about identity, not content — the single most misread result in this area.
steps.expect: Still only main, even though release/1.1 now has the identical change.

steps.title: Ask the content question instead
steps.why: `git cherry <upstream> <head>` compares patches rather than shas. A `-` means 'this commit has an equivalent on the other side'; a `+` means it is genuinely missing. This is the right tool for backport auditing.
steps.expect: The fix is marked `-` on release/1.1 — main already has an equivalent. The 'Cut release' commits are marked `+`, because those really are unique to the release branches.

steps.title: Count how far behind each branch is
steps.why: `rev-list --left-right --count` prints two numbers: commits unique to each side. It is the machine-readable version of 'ahead 3, behind 7' and belongs in any release dashboard.

steps.title: Audit every branch at once
steps.why: `for-each-ref` with a format string turns branch state into a table. This is the query you script when 'which branches need the patch' has to be answered weekly rather than once.
commands: sh -c 'for b in $(git for-each-ref --format="%(refname:short)" refs/heads); do echo "$b: $(git cherry main $b | grep -c "^+") commits not in main"; done'

verify.label: all three branches are visible to the audit
release/1.1 was backported
verify.hint: git cherry-pick the fix onto release/1.1

verify.label: release/1.0 was deliberately left alone — it is the branch still needing attention
git cherry marks the backported fix as already present, despite the different sha
verify.hint: cherry compares patch ids, not shas — that is why it sees the backport

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git branch --contains $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="timing attack" main) | wc -l'
verify.label: …while --contains still lists only main, because the sha differs

pitfalls: `--contains` answers reachability, not 'has this change'. After a cherry-pick or rebase the shas differ and the answer looks wrong.
`git cherry` compares patch ids, so it survives cherry-picks and rebases — but a conflict resolved differently on the other branch breaks the match.
`branch --merged` without an argument uses HEAD, so the answer changes depending on which branch you are standing on. Always name the branch explicitly.
Remote branches need `-r` or `-a`. `git branch --contains <sha>` alone will not mention origin's branches at all.
cheatsheet: branches from which the commit is reachable
